the-paper-money-problem.core: Startup equity is 'paper money': valuable on paper but unsellable until an IPO, acquisition or approved secondary sale. Meanwhile you may owe exercise costs and taxes, and value can be wiped out by down rounds or liquidation preferences. Plan finances around cash, not paper wealth.

first_principles.problem: An engineer with $2M of paper equity can't afford a house deposit and owes tax on options exercised.
truths: Taxes can be due before liquidity.
derivation: Know **exercise costs and tax** before acting.

analogy.title: Owning a rare painting you can't sell
analogy.story: It's 'worth' a lot, but you can't pay rent with it.
analogy.breaks: Paintings rarely lose all value; startup equity often does.

example.title: Net worth reality check
flow: After preferences in a modest exit: $300k

check.q: Why can a liquidation preference reduce employee payouts?
check.a: Preferred investors are paid back first (often 1× or more), leaving less for common shareholders in modest exits.

secondary-markets-tender-offers.core: Before an IPO, employees may get liquidity through tender offers (company-organised buybacks or investor purchases at a set price) or secondary markets (platforms like Forge or EquityZen), subject to company approval and right of first refusal. Prices may be at a discount, and tax treatment varies.

first_principles.problem: An employee needs cash from startup shares years before any IPO.
truths: Buyers price in illiquidity and risk.

analogy.title: Selling concert tickets through the official resale exchange
analogy.story: You can sell, but only through approved channels, at the price buyers will pay.
analogy.breaks: Ticket resale is common; many startups heavily restrict secondaries.

example.title: Participating in a tender
flow: Pay off debt, keep upside on 75%

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Risk reduced without giving up all upside.

check.q: What is a right of first refusal (ROFR)?
check.a: The company's right to buy your shares on the same terms before you sell them to an outside buyer.

iso-vs-nso-the-tax-taxonomy.core: In the US, Incentive Stock Options (ISOs) have no regular income tax on exercise (but the spread counts for AMT), and qualify for long-term capital gains if held 1 year after exercise and 2 years after grant. Non-qualified options (NSOs) are taxed as ordinary income on the spread at exercise. RSUs are taxed as income on vest.

first_principles.problem: An employee exercises NSOs and is shocked by a large income tax bill with no cash from the shares.
truths: Tax depends on equity type and timing.
derivation: Consider **early exercise + 83(b)** when the spread is near zero.

analogy.title: Different import categories at customs
analogy.story: The same goods are taxed differently depending on how they're classified and when you bring them in.
analogy.breaks: Customs rules are relatively stable; tax rules and thresholds change by year and country.

example.title: Exercising 10,000 options
flow: ISO: no regular tax, but $100k AMT adjustment

check.a: As ordinary income on the spread when you exercise them.

the-amt-trap-the-bankruptcy-maker.core: Exercising ISOs creates an AMT adjustment equal to the spread. If the spread is large, you can owe Alternative Minimum Tax on gains you haven't realised. If the stock then crashes (as in 2000–2001), you owe tax on value that no longer exists. Exercise in tranches below the AMT threshold, early-exercise when the spread is small, or exercise and sell in the same year.

first_principles.problem: An engineer exercises ISOs with a $1M spread, owes $250k AMT, and the company's value halves.
truths: AMT counts the ISO spread as income.
Tax is due regardless of liquidity.
derivation: Exercise in **tranches** under the AMT crossover.

analogy.title: Paying property tax on a house valued at the peak
analogy.story: The bill arrives based on last year's price, even if the market has since crashed.
analogy.breaks: Property can be sold; private shares often can't, so you can't cover the bill.

example.title: Tranche planning
flow: No AMT owed; holding periods start

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Gradual ownership without a tax shock.

check.q: Why did many engineers face AMT disasters in 2001?
check.a: They exercised ISOs at high values, owed AMT on the spread, and then the stock collapsed before they could sell.

the-90-day-clock-golden-handcuffs.core: Most option plans give you 90 days after leaving to exercise vested options or lose them. Exercising may require large cash plus taxes, which effectively traps people in jobs. Some companies offer extended exercise windows (5–10 years); check yours before deciding to leave, and plan funding.

first_principles.problem: Leaving a startup means paying $150k to exercise and cover AMT within 90 days, or forfeiting four years of options.
truths: Unexercised options expire after the window.
Exercising costs strike × shares plus taxes.
ISOs convert to NSOs after 90 days if extended.
derivation: **Negotiate** extended windows at hire or exit.

analogy.title: A store voucher that expires 90 days after you stop being a member
analogy.story: Use it or lose it, and using it costs money.
analogy.breaks: Vouchers are free to use; exercising options can cost more than a year's salary.

example.title: Pre-departure planning
flow: Ask for 5-year extension as part of exit
Or exercise half now, let half lapse

check.q: What happens to ISOs if the exercise window is extended beyond 90 days after leaving?
check.a: They lose ISO status and are treated as NSOs.
